title: Data Centers Have a New PR Plan: Your Kid’s Field Trip
gist: Industry groups like 7x24 Exchange and AFCOM, plus operators such as Sabey and Amazon, are courting children via books, kits and field trips as data center opposition grows (Pew: about half of Americans see them as mostly bad). The column also flags CoreWeave bond stress and a $3 billion Massachusetts project cancellation as signs of rising skittishness.

insights.claim: The data center industry is adding youth outreach (children's books, school kits, field trips) to its lobbying, job-creation programs and tax breaks as pushback against massive build-outs and energy-hungry campuses intensifies.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Industry spending on social-license maintenance signals local opposition is material enough to threaten project pipelines.
insights.locator: The story is part of a broader pattern

insights.claim: The nonprofit 7x24 Exchange International promotes data centers as 'mission critical' infrastructure via a children's story, an 'International Data Center Day' pitched to school administrators, crosswords, coloring pages, an evaporation science project and data-center-themed books.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Shows an organized, trade-group-run education campaign rather than isolated company PR.

insights.claim: The Potomac chapter of AFCOM sponsored Memorial Day flag-making kits for 3,100 first graders across 37 Loudoun County, Virginia schools (Data Center Alley), with a card of statistics on the industry's positive local economic impact.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Outreach is concentrated in the densest data center market, where opposition risk is highest.

insights.claim: WIRED's tally of public blogs and social posts found at least eleven companies and industry groups have hosted student field trips to local data centers since 2025, and 7x24 Exchange has visited or organized at least six K-12 events this year.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Gives a rough scale of the campaign; the count is a lower bound based on public posts.

insights.claim: Sabey, which runs seven US data centers, hosts recurring field trips and internship and mock-interview partnerships with Washington state school districts (Quincy, Manson, Eastmont), while Amazon, Microsoft, Vantage and Yahoo facilities also host student visits.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Hyperscalers and colocation operators alike are building workforce-pipeline relationships with local schools.
insights.locator: Sabey, a company that runs seven

insights.claim: A summer Pew Research poll of 10,000 Americans found about half see data centers as 'mostly bad' for the environment and quality of life, and an ideologically diverse cohort is rallying against them nationwide.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Opposition is bipartisan and broad, raising permitting and political risk for build-outs.

insights.claim: Negative sentiment toward local data centers is in some places amplified by proximity to local schools, which makes school outreach a targeted reputational defense.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Siting near schools can intensify opposition and invites countermeasures aimed at families.
insights.locator: In some places, the negative sentiment

insights.claim: Educational materials and field trips are framed as ways industries maintain their 'social license to operate' in a community, following the playbook of oil and gas (university research, K-12 STEM, pro-industry lessons in Oklahoma and Texas) and tech (STEM funding, coding in schools).
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: The analogy implies data centers may follow the same trajectory of sustained, escalating image management.

themes.theme: Critique of corporate messaging in schools

insights.claim: Alex Molnar of the National Education Policy Center says industries with image problems (fast food, tobacco, oil and gas) have brought messaging to schools for over a century, mainly to tell their 'story' rather than sell a product.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Frames the campaign as reputation management, which may invite regulatory or political backlash against school access.

insights.claim: Molnar argues a data center tour holds little intrinsic appeal for children: rows of servers, heat, noise and few workers, since few people work there once built.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: The low employment per facility undercuts the job-creation argument that the outreach pushes.
insights.quote: You're going to see miles after miles of the most boring things imaginable
insights.locator: Molnar says he doesn't get what's in it

insights.claim: Molnar believes such corporate influence should be disallowed and that districts and communities must protect children, who lack the critical ability adults have to assess messaging.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Possible policy vector: restrictions on corporate-sponsored school content could target the sector.
insights.locator: Molnar believes this kind of corporate influence

themes.theme: Data center financing and project risk

insights.claim: CoreWeave's data center-financing bonds saw a sharp selloff with a corresponding stock drop in the week, with only a slight recovery, which the column reads as increasing skittishness around the data center buildout.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Credit markets are a leading stress indicator for debt-funded AI capacity.
insights.locator: CoreWeave has been on a wild ride

insights.claim: Bloomberg reports CoreWeave's founders have sold $3.3 billion of stock since the company went public.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Large insider selling alongside bond stress is a negative signal for sentiment.
insights.locator: CoreWeave has been on a wild ride

insights.claim: Westfield, Massachusetts killed a $3 billion data center project by developer Servistar after its planning board criticized missed deadlines and slow development.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Local boards are rejecting even large projects, and execution slippage gives them grounds to do so.

insights.claim: Data centers have become the midterm season's biggest issue per the column; a protester interrupted the Maine Senate debate between Susan Collins and Troy Jackson over data center environmental impact, and Collins tried to position herself as the more anti-data center candidate.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Candidates in both parties may move to oppose data centers, raising policy risk.
